messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Jian had always prided himself on his foresight. As a policy analyst, his job was to anticipate problems, to model scenarios, and to build contingency plans. He was a man who believed in predictable outcomes derived from careful analysis. This belief was incinerated, along with his home, eight months ago during the wildfires. He and his wife, Mei, had only fifteen minutes to evacuate. He remembers the world turning a sickening orange, the acrid smell of burning pine and plastic, and a profound, choking weakness in his limbs as he stumbled through the haze, his body feeling like a stranger's. The sheer speed and unpredictability of the fire’s advance left him feeling utterly powerless, a sensation he had never before experienced.

In the months that followed, Jian’s analytical mind turned inward, trying to model and control a new, terrifying variable: himself. The world, he had concluded, was fundamentally unsafe, and he had to be constantly careful because you never know what might happen next. This core belief began to dictate his life, making him hyper-attuned to any sign of danger. The scent of a distant chimney or a neighbor’s barbecue would send a jolt of alarm through him, his mind immediately scanning for an escape route. At his government office, which was known for its fluid priorities, any last-minute meeting or sudden change in a project’s scope—things he once handled with ease—now felt like a personal threat, a sign that chaos was about to erupt again. This constant state of high alert, born from his conviction that he must always be on guard, made him exquisitely sensitive to the very triggers that reminded him of his helplessness.

Any of these triggers—the smell of smoke, a sudden change of plans, even the simple sensation of coming down with a cold—would immediately confirm his deepest fears about his own stability. When he felt the onset of a seasonal flu last month, the familiar aches and fatigue didn't just feel like illness; they felt like the same debilitating weakness he experienced fleeing the fire. The physical sensation immediately sparked the thought, *I can’t rely on myself. My own body is failing me.* This conviction that he was fundamentally unreliable was reinforced by his reactions to external events. A sudden project pivot at work last week left him so disoriented and panicked that he had to excuse himself to the restroom, splashing cold water on his face and staring at his own wide eyes in the mirror. He was certain that this intense, uncontrollable response was not normal grief or stress; it was definitive proof that he was going crazy.

This vicious cycle has left Jian feeling trapped inside his own head. The belief that he is fragile and that the world is unpredictable makes him scan constantly for threats, which in turn makes him more likely to encounter a trigger. When a trigger does occur, his intense reaction serves as evidence for his negative appraisals, further cementing his belief that he is losing his mind and cannot trust his own responses. He has started to avoid situations he can’t control, declining invitations to social gatherings and finding excuses to work from home more often, which has created a subtle but growing distance between him and Mei.

He finally sought therapy after a performance review in which his manager, while gentle, noted a decline in his adaptability and a new pattern of missing deadlines on fast-moving projects. The feedback landed like a verdict, confirming his fear that he could no longer function. Jian is terrified that the competent, analytical man he once was has been permanently replaced by this fearful, fragile stranger. He came to therapy hoping, he said, to find a way to trust himself again in a world he no longer believes is safe.
